items.title: 10.4 Motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field

source_refs.note: Topic 10.4 with Fig. 10.10, Example 10.3 and the side boxes (PDF 234-236, printed 231-233). The text cites Fig. 10.8 for the left-hand rule (Fig. 10.3); recorded.

blocks.text: A current-carrying conductor placed perpendicularly in a uniform magnetic field experiences a force F. Since a current is the flow of electric charges, this raises the question: do individual charges moving through a magnetic field also experience a force? The answer is yes; experiments show that a charged particle does experience a force when it moves across a magnetic field. We can calculate this force by examining the behaviour of a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

Consider a conductor of length L through which N charged particles, each with charge q, are passing in time t. The motion of these particles produces a current I = Q/t = Nq/t, where Q is the total charge flowing in time t. If v is the velocity of the charged particles, their velocity along the conductor is v = v L(hat), where L(hat) is the unit vector in the direction of the current. The sign of the force depends on whether q is positive or negative; L(hat) is directed along the current, which is the direction of motion of positive charges. Since the particles take time t to cross the conductor of length L, t = L/v, so I = Nq/t = Nqv/L ... (10.8).

If this conductor is placed in a uniform magnetic field B, it experiences the force F = I L x B ... (10.9). As L = L L(hat) ... (10.10), substituting I and L gives F = (Nqv/L)(L L(hat) x B), or F = Nqv L(hat) x B ... (10.11). As the velocity v is directed along the conductor, F = Nq v x B ... (10.12). Therefore the force on a single particle is F = q v x B ... (10.13).

blocks.title: Magnetic force on a moving charge
blocks.text: F = q v x B (10.13). If theta is the angle between B and v, the magnitude is F = qvB sin theta ... (10.14). The force is maximum when B is perpendicular to v (theta = 90 degrees) and zero when B is along v (theta = 0). Its direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule or the right-hand rule (Fig. 10.3, cited as Fig. 10.8 in print).

items: A positively charged particle entering the field (B into the paper) along the dotted line experiences an upward force and is deflected along a curved path (Fig. 10.10a).
A negatively charged particle is deflected downward by the force acting on it (Fig. 10.10b).

blocks.caption: Charged particles in a magnetic field and the velocity selector (original diagram after Figures 10.10 to 10.12 and topics 10.4 and 10.5).
blocks.long_description: A charge moving across a magnetic field feels a force at right angles to both its velocity and the field, so positive and negative charges bend opposite ways. Because the force is always at right angles to the velocity it changes only the direction of motion, not the speed, and in a uniform field the charge goes round a circle whose radius is the momentum divided by the charge times the field. In a velocity selector an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles push a moving charge in opposite directions; only a charge whose speed equals the electric field divided by the magnetic field feels no net force and goes straight through.

blocks.title: Example 10.3
blocks.text: An electron (printed 'election') enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly with a speed of 10^4 m s^-1. What path will it follow inside the field? (B = 2.5 Wb m^-2, m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.) Solution: F = qvB sin theta; as v is perpendicular to B, theta = 90 degrees and q = e, so F = evB. Since F acts perpendicular to v, it provides the centripetal force that keeps the electron in a circle of radius r: evB = mv^2/r, so r = mv/(eB) = (9.11 x 10^-31 kg x 10^4 m s^-1)/(1.6 x 10^-19 C x 2.5 Wb m^-2) = 2.3 x 10^-8 m. The path is a circle of radius 2.3 x 10^-8 m.

Like electric field lines, magnetic field lines never cross each other, but instead push apart from each other (Do You Know). A picture on an old television screen, computer monitor or oscilloscope becomes distorted when a bar magnet is brought near it, because the magnetic force deflects the moving electrons of the beam (Point to ponder).

blocks.caption: Force on a moving charge
rows: curved (circle combined with drift along B)

blocks.prompt: The radius of the path of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field is directly proportional to what (MCQ 10.2)? Does a uniform magnetic field change the kinetic energy of a moving charged particle (constructed response 10.5)? An electron and a proton are projected at right angles into a field with the same velocity; which is deflected more (short question 10.7)?
blocks.explanation: r = mv/(qB), so r is proportional to the momentum mv, option (b). No: the magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work; it changes the direction of motion but not the speed or kinetic energy. The electron: with the same charge and speed but a much smaller mass, its radius r = mv/(eB) is far smaller, so its path bends much more sharply.

blocks.prompt: A proton enters a field of 0.300 T at 45 degrees with a speed of 10^7 m s^-1; find the radius of its circular path (numerical 10.8). Electrons accelerated through 15 kV pass through a 0.35 T field; find the largest force on one (numerical 10.2).
blocks.explanation: Only the component of velocity across the field, v sin 45 = 7.07 x 10^6 m s^-1, causes circular motion: r = m v sin 45/(eB) = 1.67 x 10^-27 x 7.07 x 10^6/(1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.300) = 0.246 m. The electron's speed is v = sqrt(2eV/m) = sqrt(2 x 1.6 x 10^-19 x 15 000/9.11 x 10^-31) = 7.26 x 10^7 m s^-1, and the largest force (theta = 90 degrees) is evB = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 7.26 x 10^7 x 0.35 = 4.1 x 10^-12 N.

items: N charges q crossing length L in t = L/v: I = Nqv/L (10.8); F = I L x B (10.9) gives F = Nq v x B (10.12) and, for one charge, F = q v x B (10.13), F = qvB sin theta (10.14): maximum across the field, zero along it.
Positive and negative charges bend opposite ways (Fig. 10.10). The force is perpendicular to v: circular path r = mv/(qB), no change of speed. Example 10.3: r = 2.3 x 10^-8 m.
